Where it began

Gundappa Viswanath was born in Bhadravathi on 12 February 1949. He played his state cricket for Mysore, later renamed Karnataka, for his whole career.

On his first-class debut, against Andhra Pradesh in 1967, he made a double hundred. Two years later, in his first Test, against Australia at Kanpur in 1969, he made a hundred too. He was the first to do both. The same match brought him a duck as well, so he saw both ends of batting at once.

The player

Viswanath played 91 Tests for India between 1969 and 1983. He scored 6,080 runs at 41.93, with 14 hundreds, 35 fifties and a top score of 222. A regular at slip, he held 63 catches. He played one-day internationals between 1974 and 1982, and took part in two World Cups, in 1975 and 1979.

He was at his best in the middle of the 1970s. At Madras in 1974–75, facing a West Indies attack that included Andy Roberts, he made 97 not out in a total of 190, and India won. The Wisden 100 later placed it 38th on its list of the greatest innings, and second among those that stopped short of a hundred. A year on, at Port of Spain, his 112 helped India chase 403, at that time the highest target ever reached to win a Test.

What made him special

He relied on timing and supple wrists rather than brute force. He could play every shot, but his favourite was the square cut, and fast bowlers saw a great deal of it. He tended to shine when the pitch was difficult and the bowling was quick, and he was at his happiest against the strong pace attacks of Australia and West Indies. Bowling was another matter. He took one Test wicket, at a cost of 46 runs, and was wise enough to leave the rest of that work to others.

He led India in two Tests in 1979–80. In the Golden Jubilee Test against England he called Bob Taylor back to bat after the umpire had already sent him on his way. Taylor went on to make runs that helped England win. It was a sporting gesture, and it says a good deal about him.

Away from the middle

To cricket fans he was simply Vishy. In 1978 his India teammate Sunil Gavaskar also became his brother-in-law, so the family had two Test cricketers to talk about.

After leaving Tests in 1983 he gave a great deal back to the game. He was an ICC match referee from 1999 to 2004, chaired India's national selectors, managed the Indian team, coached at the National Cricket Academy and was vice-president of his state association in Karnataka. He received the Padma Shri in 1971, the Arjuna Award in 1977–78 and, later, the C. K. Nayudu Lifetime Achievement Award.

And finally

Plenty of batters chase hundreds. One of Viswanath's most admired innings finished three runs short of one, and it is rated above a great many that got there. Winning, it seems, was the part that counted.
